Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy C-22 because these alloys are difficult to machine by conventional methods. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The physical and mechanical properties of the tool electrode therefore have a direct influence on process efficiency, dimensional accuracy, and the characteristics of the machined surface. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Electrode material choice thus shapes both the economic and technical outcomes of EDM operations. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

One principal concern in EDM is electrode wear: the relative loss of tool material during spark erosion affects electrode life, dimensional fidelity of features (for example square holes), and the need for frequent electrode replacement or re-machining. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)(Shastri et al. 2022) Process parameters such as discharge current and pulse duration play an important role in driving electrode wear and in altering electrode geometry at the tool ends. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024)

The second major concern surveyed in this review is surface integrity after EDM. High tool wear rate, low material removal rate, and elevated surface roughness are recurring challenges that also relate to the condition of the machined surface, including recast layer formation. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022) Studies have shown that machining parameters—most notably peak current and pulse-on time—are among the dominant factors controlling material removal rate and average surface roughness. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022)

Recent work highlights the growing use of graphite electrodes and the importance of graphite grain size: finer-grained graphite can improve process efficiency and reduce tool wear, while coarser grains may increase material removal but at the expense of higher relative tool wear and altered discharge stability. (Nowicki et al. 2024)(Nowicki et al. 2022) Understanding these trade-offs between electrode wear, process efficiency, and surface integrity is central to optimizing EDM of Hastelloy and related nickel-based superalloys.

Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is extensively applied to nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy because these alloys are difficult to machine by conventional cutting methods. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The choice of electrode material therefore strongly influences both the economic and technical outcomes of EDM: the electrode’s physical and mechanical properties affect process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Electrode wear is a primary concern because tool material loss alters electrode geometry, which in turn changes spark conditions, reduces dimensional accuracy, and may increase machining time and cost. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Surface integrity of the machined part is the second major concern: EDM produces recast layers, roughness, and thermally affected zones whose extent depends on discharge energy and process stability. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Liew et al. 2020)

Experimental studies on electrode material and microstructure give specific evidence for how electrode choice and process parameters govern these outcomes. Studies comparing graphite electrodes with different grain sizes (POCO AF-5, 1 µm; POCO S-180/EDM-180, 10 µm) report that coarser-grained graphite yields higher material removal rates (higher process efficiency) but with greater relative tool wear, whereas finer-grained graphite produces lower surface roughness (Ra) and reduced tool wear under comparable conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) The mechanism proposed is that finer graphite grains detach less and promote more stable electrical discharges, while larger grains detach more readily and destabilize the discharge, increasing MRR but accelerating electrode degradation. (Nowicki et al. 2024)(Nowicki et al. 2022)

Beyond electrode microstructure, discharge energy parameters—particularly peak current and pulse duration—are repeatedly identified as the dominant drivers of MRR and Ra: experiments indicate that peak current and pulse-on time largely determine both removal efficiency and surface finish. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nas & Kara 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024) Statistical analysis in one study quantified the influence of peak current as the single most effective factor for Ra and MRR, contributing 74.79% and 86.43% of the explained variance respectively, with optimal Ra and MRR observed at lower peak current (6 A) and shorter pulse-on time (300 µs) for the cryogenically treated sample in that experiment. (Nas & Kara 2022) Relative tool wear, however, was found to be most sensitive to the time interval parameter in the graphite experiments, indicating that off-time or inter-pulse timing controls electrode degradation rate under those conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

Process instability and thermal diffusion further explain how parameter choices translate into wear and surface damage: high currents and long pulses produce unstable sparks and concentrated heat diffusion that transform sharp electrode features (for example, square electrode ends) into rounded or hemispherical shapes and increase electrode material loss, while also promoting larger recast zones and rougher surfaces on the workpiece. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)(Shastri et al. 2022)

Because EDM of nickel-based superalloys thus involves trade-offs between MRR, tool wear rate (TWR), and surface integrity, researchers have explored auxiliary approaches—cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed EDM, ultrasonic assistance, and combinations thereof—to mitigate high TWR, low MRR, and poor surface finish. (Shastri et al. 2022) These interventions change the effective thermal and electrical conditions at the discharge and have been evaluated alongside electrode material and parameter studies to identify parameter sets that balance efficiency and surface quality. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy, which are difficult to cut by conventional means. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The EDM process removes material by electrical discharges between the workpiece and a tool electrode; consequently, the physical and mechanical properties of the electrode directly influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) 

The choice of electrode material therefore shapes both the cost and the quality of the process. Graphite electrodes are increasingly used because of low purchase cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature—properties that make graphite commercially attractive for EDM tooling. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Recent work highlights that graphite microstructure (grain size) further conditions performance: fine-grained graphite (1 µm POCO AF-5) and coarser graphite (10 µm POCO S-180 / EDM-180) show systematic differences in material removal effectiveness, tool wear behaviour, and resulting surface roughness on Hastelloy C-22. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) 

Electrode wear is one of the main concerns. Studies report that graphite with larger grains yields higher process efficiency (higher MRR) but at the cost of increased relative tool wear, whereas finer-grained graphite achieves lower surface roughness and can reduce tool wear under some conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) Mechanistically, detached graphite grains alter discharge stability: grain detachment from the electrode can destabilize the electrical discharges and thus change removal efficiency and wear patterns. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Experimental analyses identify the principal electrical parameters that drive these outcomes—discharge current and pulse duration dominate material removal rate and average surface roughness, while the time interval (pulse-off time) is reported as the dominant factor affecting relative electrode wear for graphite electrodes. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) 

Other process and material conditions also modulate electrode wear and surface quality. Investigations that modify workpiece metallurgy by cryogenic treatments (shallow and deep cryogenic treatment) show that peak current, pulse-on time, and the material condition jointly determine Ra and MRR, with peak current often the most influential factor in ANOVA analyses. (Nas & Kara 2022) Moreover, process instability and heat diffusion during EDM can produce pronounced shape changes at electrode edges—sharp square electrode ends can round into hemispherical forms due to unstable sparks and thermal diffusion—so current and pulse duration are again implicated in driving electrode wear geometry. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) 

Surface integrity after machining is the second concern this review examines. EDM commonly produces high surface roughness and altered surface layers (recast layers), and the combination of high tool wear rate and unstable sparking contributes to these effects. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024) Strategies documented to mitigate adverse surface integrity and wear include process variants such as cryogenic cooling/treatment, powder-mixed EDM, ultrasonic assistance, and combined techniques; these modifications have been studied for their effects on MRR, TWR, Ra, and recast-layer characteristics. (Shastri et al. 2022) Finally, related technologies that use electrical discharges to deposit or modify surface layers (electrical discharge coating) indicate additional routes to control surface characteristics, though their specific application to Hastelloy EDM requires targeted investigation. (Liew et al. 2020)

Studies comparing graphite electrodes with different grain sizes report that coarser graphite grains tend to increase process efficiency (higher MRR) but also produce higher relative tool wear, whereas fine‑grained graphite yields lower surface roughness and reduced tool wear under comparable conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) The mechanism proposed for these effects is that detached graphite grains influence the stability of electrical discharges: grain detachment alters discharge conditions at the interelectrode gap and thus modifies both removal efficiency and the evolution of the machined surface. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Parametric sensitivity studies identify the electrical parameters that drive these outcomes. Discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration are reported as the main factors determining MRR and Ra in graphite‑electrode EDM experiments, with some analyses showing peak current to be the dominant factor for both Ra and MRR. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nas & Kara 2022) Time interval (the off‑time) has been identified specifically as the dominant parameter influencing the relative wear of graphite electrodes in at least one experimental study. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Across other investigations, current and pulse duration are also implicated in producing unstable sparks that reshape electrode geometry and accelerate wear, for example converting sharp electrode features into hemispherical ends under certain conditions. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

rows.b: Selective laser melting (SLM) is a laser-based powder-bed fusion method that can produce near‑dense, near‑net‑shape metal parts layer‑by‑layer, and has been used to fabricate maraging steel components with complex geometry directly from powder (Yap et al. 2015). The rapid, localized melting and solidification inherent to SLM produces characteristic microstructural features in maraging/precipitation‑hardening steels — such as very fine submicron grains, hierarchical (sub)grains and in‑situ precipitates — that distinguish additively manufactured material from conventionally produced counterparts and can enhance strength, wear and corrosion performance in some cases (Tan et al. 2018)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). Post‑printing heat treatments (for example solution treatment, aging, tempering or intercritical treatments) substantially modify these as‑built microstructures by inducing precipitation, relieving residual stresses, enabling martensite↔austenite reversion and altering precipitate morphology and distribution; consequently, mechanical properties and corrosion‑related responses change with the chosen thermal cycle and its parameters (temperature, time, prior condition) (Tan et al. 2018)(Godec et al. 2021)(Khan et al. 2022). Although some studies have explicitly characterized corrosion or corrosion‑related performance of SLM maraging steels — for example by comparing corrosion after plasma nitriding with and without prior heat treatments, and by measuring pitting behaviour in chloride solutions following intercritical tempering — the influence of specific microstructural changes (such as reversed austenite formation, local elemental redistribution during precipitate dissolution, or the presence of processing‑induced defects) on corrosion resistance remains less comprehensively studied than mechanical strength and fatigue behavior, and results vary with the thermal and surface treatments applied (Godec et al. 2021)(Khan et al. 2022)(Tan et al. 2018)(Afkhami et al. 2019).
